blocks.text: Penicillin is a powerful antibiotic used to treat many kinds of bacterial infection, such as respiratory infections like strep throat, pneumonia, scarlet fever and sinusitis. It also helps to treat skin and soft-tissue infections such as cellulitis and erysipelas.

The structure of penicillin contains two core rings: a four-membered beta-lactam ring and a five-membered thiazolidine ring, both with side chains attached. The beta-lactam ring is crucial for the antibiotic's activity; it is also the site where bacterial enzymes called beta-lactamases can attack and deactivate penicillin.

Penicillin is mistaken for its normal building block by the bacterial enzyme that strengthens the cell wall. The enzyme takes up the penicillin molecule, the beta-lactam ring opens, and penicillin binds permanently to the enzyme, which is inactivated. The bacteria keep growing, but without a functional cell wall they eventually burst and die. Human cells have no cell wall, so penicillin does not harm our cells.

blocks.alt: Left: the penicillin core. A square beta-lactam ring (orange) with a C=O group shares its nitrogen with a five-membered thiazolidine ring (blue) containing S, a carbon with two CH3 groups and a carbon bearing COOH; an NH-CO-R side chain is attached to the square ring. Right: four boxes: the cell-wall enzyme takes up penicillin; the beta-lactam ring opens and binds permanently, blocking the enzyme; the bacterium grows without a working wall and bursts; human cells have no wall and are not harmed.
blocks.caption: Penicillin: structure and action (original diagram; the structure is redrawn after Figure 32.2).
blocks.long_description: The strained four-membered beta-lactam ring is the reactive part. When it opens inside the enzyme, penicillin stays bonded to the enzyme and the bacterium can no longer build its wall.

blocks.title: Did you know?
blocks.text: In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin by accident when he noticed that mould growing on a contaminated petri dish had killed the surrounding bacteria. The mould, later identified as Penicillium, released a substance that stopped bacterial growth. This chance observation led to the first antibiotic and changed modern medicine.
